name: Jade Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, government or political parties, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from your private thoughts. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Jade, 58, a junior helping the qualified electrician wire and repair homes and businesses. I worked at an alterations counter before the owner sold up, then took a vocational certificate; I'm still below the experienced crew for skill and speed, with no electrician's licence or sign-off authority. This firm pays above the usual rate, my partner drives a forklift, and we have a mortgage, grown children living elsewhere and twelve months of expenses saved. There are plenty of electrical employers nearby, and I use AI occasionally for a checked note after a colleague has demonstrated it; retirement is a question we need actual income figures for, not a funded date I've chosen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say keep the little tools that have earned their place. I use AI occasionally for a draft note after a colleague has shown me it works, with the senior checking it. I'd rather ask again about the drawing than nod at a tidy sentence I hadn't understood.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our current wages cover the bills and mortgage, and we have twelve months of expenses saved. This firm pays above the usual rate, and there are plenty of other electrical employers nearby. I'm still junior, but this mild picture doesn't make our own living feel threatened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the paid supervised tasks actually offered. Starting now I'd ask the qualified electrician to check my understanding of an unclear instruction before I repeated the task. Through the first year we'd keep our ordinary household budget and existing reserve, not treat a quiet AI story as a pension award.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about our money, with normal frustration about being a beginner. I like finishing a small bit neatly after someone has checked it. I don't need to pretend the household is poor to admit I still need help at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What brought you to electrical work at 58?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I worked for years at an alterations counter, then took a vocational certificate when the owner sold up and I wanted a change. I'm slower and less skilled than the experienced electricians, and my tasks need their supervision. A straight seam doesn't tell me which mark on a wiring drawing matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who is part of your household now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner drives a forklift, our children are grown and live elsewhere, and we have a mortgage. The reserve came from years of two wages before this change of work. I'd like to understand when retirement could be affordable, but I have no confirmed amount or date to build a stopping plan around.

say: I'd keep **proven small tools** and ask about anything I hadn't understood.
I'd value a **checked instruction** more than a tidy sentence that tempted me to nod along.
think: Our **regular wages** cover the mortgage and bills, with twelve months saved and plenty of nearby electrical employers.
My **higher pay** supports security without making me skilled or confirming an affordable retirement date.
do: Keep **offered paid supervised tasks** through the first year.
Request a **qualified understanding check** before repeating an unfamiliar task.
Retain the **ordinary budget** and reserve, counting no unconfirmed pension or grown child's earnings.
feel: **Calm** about household living, while recognising that financial comfort doesn't remove a beginner's need for help.
S0.quote: A straight seam doesn't tell me which mark on a wiring drawing matters.
fieldNote: Her **former sewing work** supplies experience outside this trade, not an electrical licence, independent authority or skill above the junior profile.
Her **strong finances** remain real in higher pay and a year-long reserve, while retirement eligibility and income are still unconfirmed.

steps.text: Keep offered paid supervised tasks and ask for qualified checks before unfamiliar work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a faster plan should still leave time for somebody to show the beginner what it means. I'd try a new aid after a colleague had demonstrated it on work we knew. I'd want the company to check actual mistakes, not just tell us the screen was friendly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own paid days could shrink if quicker planning meant fewer helpers, even though most of my tasks were still physical. My partner's forklift work is physical too, but that doesn't make a cut in my wage harmless. A year saved gives us time to react, not a reason to ignore what the weekly pay says.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request a two-session trial of the approved AI picture organiser after a completed-job demonstration, only in paid time with no personal fee and normal weekly wages and hours unchanged. I'd use practice material and have the qualified electrician check it before any output reached actual work. In the first year I'd keep supervised tasks and review both household wages monthly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the wage, and willing to see whether a proven aid helped. I don't need to defend a bad system or my first dislike of it. I'd like the actual result explained in words I can use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if a picture was put in the wrong group?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the example and ask the qualified electrician to compare it with the original job. I wouldn't treat an automatically chosen group as a technical instruction. Looking organised isn't the same as being checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay a trial fee or practise unpaid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd ask for a paid approved slot with no personal charge, or keep the existing method. I can afford a choice without thinking the firm should charge beginners for required practice. Our reserve isn't the company's training budget.

I'd ask for **demonstrated results** and real error checks before trusting a new aid.
think: My **paid helper days** could shrink even while the tasks remain mainly physical.
Our **year-long reserve** provides response time, not a reason to dismiss a realistic fall in my wage.
do: Request **AI picture sorting** for two approved sessions after demonstration, only free in paid time with normal weekly wages and hours unchanged.
Use **practice material** and require qualified checks before output reaches actual work, stopping any wrongly grouped example.
Keep **supervised tasks** and review actual household wages monthly during the first year.
feel: **Anxious** about paid days, with enough security to examine a demonstrated aid rather than rush or refuse automatically.
S1.quote: Our reserve isn't the company's training budget.
fieldNote: Her **new learning** is a distinct approved picture-organising trial, rather than relabelling the occasional note tool she already uses.
The **trial boundaries** preserve paid time, fees, normal wages and hours, practice data and qualified checks without granting electrical decision authority.

steps.text: Request two approved AI picture-sorting sessions after a completed-job demonstration
Practise only free during paid time with normal weekly wages and hours unchanged
Use practice material only; require qualified checks before real work and stop wrongly grouped examples
Keep supervised tasks and review actual household wages monthly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI arrives in 2028 at my age 60, then capable robots around 2031 at 63. The extra years for physical work are time to prepare, not a promise that helpers are protected. I'd ask what work was actually paid rather than decide a birthday had become my income plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My helper hours could fall once robots compete for simple physical tasks, and my partner's forklift work could change too. I don't know how quickly either employer would buy machines. Twelve months saved gives us room to test another way of earning without pretending it replaces a wage or guarantees retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer at most two monthly Saturday mending orders using my existing sewing skills only with employer permission, required approvals and insurance, and all setup costs within 200 spare wages. My partner would need to agree, the twelve-month reserve would stay untouched and later costs would come only from actual receipts, stopping if those conditions failed. In 2029 I'd keep only paid supervised work actually offered within my ability and request available budget help to check retirement income figures rather than assume a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about later earnings, but able to try a small thing without betting the house. A pair of paid hems wouldn't pay for the rest of our lives. I want a test I can stop, not a new story I have to keep funding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if insurance or permissions cost more than the 200 limit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The test wouldn't start. The cap covers all setup costs, not just thread, and the money must be genuinely spare after ordinary bills. I wouldn't use the old reserve or borrow to make the first two orders possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would mending stay safe from the same robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, physical sewing could face that capability too. I'd test actual local demand while there was paid work, not call an old skill a permanent shelter. I'd request actual retirement eligibility, amounts and dates before any household decision about stopping.

say: I'd separate **thinking AI at 60** from robots around 63 and avoid promising protection for physical helpers.
I'd ask about **actual paid work** rather than turn a birthday into an income plan.
think: Both **physical household jobs** could lose hours, while machine prices and employer purchase timing remain unknown.
Our **twelve-month reserve** allows a small earning test, not lifetime replacement wages or a confirmed pension.
do: Offer up to two **monthly orders** only with employer permission, required approvals, insurance and all setup within 200 spare wages.
Stop if **permissions or consent** fail; protect the reserve, borrow nothing and fund later costs only from money actually received.
Keep **offered paid supervised work** within ability in 2029 and request available help checking actual retirement income rather than assume eligibility.
feel: **Anxious** about later income, with resources for a limited test and no belief that two orders fund retirement.
S2.quote: A pair of paid hems wouldn't pay for the rest of our lives.
fieldNote: The **mending test** uses a skill she actually has, with permissions, insurance, a spare-wage cap, partner consent and an untouched reserve.
She rejects **permanent physical shelter** and counts only real receipts, while advice, retirement eligibility and later employment remain unconfirmed.

steps.text: Cap all setup at 200 spare wages; start only with employer permission, required approvals and insurance
Limit monthly orders to two with partner consent, reserve untouched and money received covering later costs
Keep only offered paid supervised work within actual ability in 2029
Request available budget help to check actual retirement eligibility amounts and dates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets me see whether an idea pays before I need to rely on it. Thinking AI arrives at 63 in 2031 and robots around 66 in 2034. I'd still keep any mending work small until actual demand and costs proved the point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect our current wages to stay steady over the next few years, with a strong reserve and plenty of firms nearby. I don't know whether we'd have enough confirmed income to stop before the physical change. The extra time helps the checking without promising a body or a paid job at 64.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer at most two monthly mending orders with employer permission, approvals, insurance, partner consent and total setup within 200 spare wages, leaving the reserve untouched. I'd keep currently offered paid supervised tasks within ability, funding later mending costs only from receipts and stopping if conditions failed. In 2032 my partner and I would check actual resources, orders and capacity before any continued work or exit, with exit only if affordable and agreed rather than assumed from age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later income, but secure enough now to compare real figures. I'd rather discover a poor business idea with two orders than after calling it my pension. The course of the next few years isn't a promise of the next twenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you count mending income before somebody paid?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd count actual money received after costs. An interested neighbour isn't a paid order. If the work didn't cover ongoing costs, or the permissions or my partner's agreement failed, I'd stop rather than use the reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the plan require you to work on electrical sites at 64?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, we'd use actual offers, my ability and whatever supervision a task required. The vocational certificate doesn't become a licence through the passing of six years. I wouldn't invent a wage to make the later budget look balanced.

I'd keep **mending small** while costs and payments establish what it really contributes.
think: Our **near-term wages** look steady, with a strong reserve and plentiful local employers.
I still lack confirmed **stopping resources**, and extra years guarantee neither future work nor the body to do it.
do: Offer up to two **monthly orders** only with permissions, insurance, partner consent and total setup within 200 spare wages, preserving the reserve.
Keep **current supervised work** within ability, funding later mending costs only from receipts and stopping if its conditions fail.
Review **2032 resources and capacity** with my partner; consider exit only if affordable and agreed, assuming no job or pension.
feel: **Uneasy** about later income, with current security and a small test kept separate from any claim to fund retirement.
S3.quote: An interested neighbour isn't a paid order.
fieldNote: Her **business limit** persists across the longer warning, and actual paid receipts rather than customer interest decide continuation.
Her **2032 review** uses actual offers and capacity; an exit requires affordability and partner agreement rather than an assumed licence or pension.

steps.text: Cap all setup at 200 spare wages; start only with employer permission, required approvals and insurance
Limit monthly orders to two with partner consent, reserve untouched and money received covering later costs
Keep only currently offered paid supervised tasks within actual ability

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives the grown children time to see us make decisions without pretending one forecast answers every family. Thinking AI comes at 68 in 2036 and robots around 71 in 2039. I'd want the facts about living costs before declaring either work or retirement the answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our current wages and year-long reserve make the next few years feel secure. I don't know whether we'd be able to stop before 2036 or still need income, and I won't use our children's wages as a missing line. The later physical-work question stays with me without making the next mortgage payment a crisis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer at most two permitted monthly mending jobs now only within the 200 spare-wage setup cap, with insurance, partner consent, the reserve untouched and later costs covered by actual receipts. I'd keep currently offered paid supervised tasks only within my ability. In 2037 we'd check confirmed resources, actual orders and capacity before choosing any manageable paid option or an exit, with no exit unless the real budget was affordable and my partner agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about later life, but comfortable enough to enjoy the family now. I don't need to turn every hobby skill into a retirement promise. I'd like to make an honest choice rather than spend a decade defending a cheerful one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you assume you could still mend at 69?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I'd check the actual work, my capacity and whether orders and permission still existed then. Sewing is physical work too. I won't promise the family a working pair of hands for whatever years the budget leaves blank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if a grown child offered help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask what they wanted to offer and whether they could afford the time or money, then discuss it rather than assume it continued. They don't owe us a fixed amount for being our children. Our budget would start with confirmed resources, not a parent-shaped claim on someone else's future.

I'd ask about **living costs** before deciding whether later work or stopping is affordable.

I can't assume **child payments**, a job at 69 or even continued mending capacity fills the future gap.

Keep **offered supervised paid tasks** now only within actual ability.
Check **2037 resources and capacity** with my partner; consider exit only with confirmed affordability and agreement, assuming no guaranteed work or pension.
feel: **Uneasy** about later uncertainty, with present security and no claim that a small physical sideline lasts forever.
S4.quote: I don't need to turn every hobby skill into a retirement promise.
fieldNote: She extends **physical uncertainty** to sewing as well as electrical work, so the sideline never becomes guaranteed income at 69.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots around 2031 could affect both physical-work incomes before we'd checked a real route to stop or keep earning. Clear paid hours, practical paid teaching and actual retirement figures would help. I'd also want costs and permissions clear before calling a small side job an answer to a large wage question.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether someone's old skill is being mistaken for their new qualification. I can mend a sleeve and still need an electrician to explain the drawing. I'd like the small earning test judged by money received, not by how reassuring it sounds beside the word retirement.

headlineQuote: I can mend a sleeve and still need an electrician to explain the drawing.
portrait: **Jade, 58**, is a junior with a vocational certificate, below-average electrical skill and qualified supervision after years at an alterations counter.
She has **higher pay**, a year saved, plenty of local firms, a forklift-driving partner, grown children and a mortgage.
She uses **AI occasionally** after demonstration, while new picture practice requires paid time, no personal fee and qualified checks.
Her **mending test** requires permissions, insurance, partner consent, a 200 spare-wage cap and an untouched reserve; later income remains unconfirmed.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves less checking time before robots around 2031 could affect both adults' physical-work wages.
whatWouldHelp: Clear **paid hours and teaching** plus actual retirement income figures would support usable decisions.
Real **costs and permissions** would help test a small sideline without pretending it replaces a large household wage.
